quarters:Barri Vell.name: Barri Vell
quarters:Barri Vell.teaser: The old town climbs the hill in stone stairs, from the Roman road to the steep lanes below Sant Feliu
quarters:Barri Vell.story: Rome planted Gerunda here around 77 BCE, a garrison on the road that became the Via Augusta, and the Barri Vell still climbs that same promontory on the Onyar's east bank. Carrer de la Força runs along the old line of the road; everything else is stairs. Towards the north the lanes drop steeply around the basilica of Sant Feliu, shaded even at noon, then open onto the square below the cathedral's Baroque flight. The cathedral, the baths, the walls and Sant Feliu each have their own card: this one is for getting lost between them.
quarters:Barri Vell.why: Walk it before ten, while the stone is cool and the steps are empty of tour groups.
facts: Stone stairways, Carrer de la Força and the lanes around Sant Feliu, all on foot
Before 10:00, and again in the early evening
The cathedral steps and the basilica of Sant Feliu (each has its own card under Culture); the lioness column on Carrer dels Calderers (its story belongs to El Cul de la Lleona)

Normal on Plaça de l'Oli; Fonda Cal Ros on Carrer de la Cort Reial; Dit i Fet below Sant Feliu; Zanpanzar when it is late; a xuixo at Can Castelló; xocolata desfeta at Xocolateria L'Antiga on Plaça del Vi

quarters:El Call.name: El Call
quarters:El Call.teaser: Stepped black-stone passages off Carrer de la Força, where Nachmanides was born in 1194
quarters:El Call.story: Turn off Carrer de la Força and the street gives way to narrow stepped passages, some barely shoulder-wide, climbing between tall stone houses with the sky a thin strip overhead. This was the Call, home of Girona's Jewish community until the expulsion of 1492, and one of the best-preserved medieval Jewish quarters in Europe. Nachmanides, Bonastruc ça Porta, was born here in 1194 and made the town Spain's first centre of Kabbalah. Dead ends are part of it: here the wrong turning is usually the right one. The Call museum has its own card under Culture.
quarters:El Call.why: Wear soles that grip: the old stone polishes to glass after rain.
facts: The stepped alleys and courtyards off Carrer de la Força
Early morning, before the walking tours arrive
The Museu d'Història dels Jueus in the Centre Bonastruc ça Porta (its own card under Culture)
Fonda Cal Ros and Cal Formatger on Carrer de la Cort Reial, a few minutes downhill; SAFO by Plaça del Vi for natural wine and share plates

quarters:Sant Pere de Galligants.name: Sant Pere de Galligants
quarters:Sant Pere de Galligants.teaser: The quiet north end of the old town, where a stream meets the walls and a Romanesque abbey sits on the bank
quarters:Sant Pere de Galligants.story: North of the cathedral the Barri Vell loosens. The lanes run down to the Galligants, the smallest of Girona's four rivers, and to the Romanesque abbey that takes its name from it. In the eleventh and twelfth centuries this was one of the new burgs that grew outside the old city on its northern side, joined to Pedret by a new bridge over the Galligants finished around 1200. Today it is a quarter of low stone houses, garden walls and the sound of water, a few minutes and a world away from the cathedral steps. The abbey and the Arab baths each have their own card.
quarters:Sant Pere de Galligants.why: Come here when the cathedral square is full: the north end stays quiet even in May.
facts: The streets along the Galligants below the walls, and the quiet after the cathedral crowds
Late afternoon, when the low sun reaches the abbey's stone
The abbey of Sant Pere de Galligants and the Arab baths (each has its own card under Culture)
Dit i Fet on Carrer dels Calderers; König Sandwiches on Plaça Sant Feliu for something fast; Sunset Jazz Club by Pou Rodó for a drink and live jazz afterwards

quarters:The Onyar riverfront.name: The Onyar riverfront
quarters:The Onyar riverfront.teaser: Two banks of ochre, rust and pink houses facing each other across the water, the seam between the two Gironas
quarters:The Onyar riverfront.story: The cases de l'Onyar turn their backs on the old streets and their faces to the river: tall, narrow houses with balconies and washing lines hanging straight over the water. Their colours, ochre, rust, saffron and pink, were picked when the fronts were restored in 1983 and 1984, and on a still morning the whole row repeats itself upside down in the river. This strip is the seam of the city, the Barri Vell on one bank and the Mercadal on the other, with the footbridges stitching them together. The bridges have their own walk card: this is where to stand, eat and look.
quarters:The Onyar riverfront.why: See the houses from both banks: from the west the cathedral rises behind them, from the east the reflections face you.
facts: The coloured river houses and their reflections in the Onyar
Early morning for a still river; dusk when the windows light up
The Onyar bridges walk, including the 1877 Pont de les Peixateries Velles (its own card under Walks)
Casa Cacao on Plaça Catalunya, over the river; Rocambolesc on Carrer de Santa Clara; Restaurant 8de7 near the Peixateries Velles footbridge for the set lunch menu

quarters:Mercadal.name: Mercadal
quarters:Mercadal.teaser: The flat bank across the river: the 1944 market hall, the arcaded square and the shopping streets
quarters:Mercadal.story: Cross any bridge westward and the ground goes flat. The Mercadal grew in the Middle Ages as Girona's market ground outside the walls, and it still feeds the city: the Mercat del Lleó, a 1944 hall of about sixty stalls, opens at seven and is picked over by mid-morning. A few streets north the Plaça de la Independència closes in a rectangle of nineteenth-century arcades, and the pedestrian streets around Santa Clara carry the shops. This is where Girona lives on weekdays, with shopping bags, school runs and coffee at the bar. The Devesa park lies beyond, with its own walk card.
quarters:Mercadal.why: Do the market before nine, then take your coffee under the arcades of the square.
facts: The Mercat del Lleó, the arcaded Plaça de la Independència and the shopping streets
Early morning for the market, closed on Sundays
The fish counters of the Mercat del Lleó before ten
Can Marquès beside the market; Casa Marieta on Plaça de la Independència; Divinum and Nexe for a serious dinner; Restaurant Massana towards the Devesa

quarters:Pedret.name: Pedret
quarters:Pedret.teaser: The old road out of town to the north, where the river heads for the Ter
quarters:Pedret.story: Pedret is the long street-village that leads out of the old town to the north, below the cliffs of the Barri Vell. It grew as one of the medieval burgs beyond the walls, joined to Sant Pere over the Galligants around 1200, and it still has the feel of a road out: low houses, workshops, the river on one side. Just beyond, the Onyar runs past the site of the old Pedret mill into the Ter, at the edge of the Devesa, where Girona's rivers meet. Come for a walk, not a meal: El Celler de Can Roca, often placed here, stands west of the centre in Taialà.
quarters:Pedret.why: Walk it north to see where the Onyar ends and the city's four-river geography makes sense.
facts: A walk along the old road north and down to where the Onyar joins the Ter
Morning, before the heat on the riverbank
Sant Pere de Galligants on the way in (its own card under Culture)
No kept table in the quarter itself: El Celler de Can Roca and the family's Can Roca bar are west in Taialà; Esperit Roca is ten kilometres north at Sant Julià de Ramis

quarters:La Devesa.name: La Devesa
quarters:La Devesa.teaser: Catalonia's largest urban park, a grid of tall plane trees that turns into the fairground every autumn
quarters:La Devesa.story: West of the Mercadal the city gives way to the Devesa, the largest urban park in Catalonia: some 2,500 plane trees planted in straight rows in the nineteenth century, so tall that the gravel avenues stay in shade through an August afternoon, several degrees cooler than the streets. On Tuesdays and Saturdays the open-air Mercat de la Devesa sets up nearby, its pitch moving with the season. At the end of October the avenues fill with rides and stalls for the Fires de Sant Narcís, which run 23 October to 1 November in 2026. The Fires and the Devesa walk have their own cards.
quarters:La Devesa.why: Come for the shade on a hot day; this week, come for the fairground lights.
facts: Plane-tree shade, a bench and a book; the fairground in late October
Afternoon in summer, when the rest of the city bakes
The Fires de Sant Narcís fairground, 23 October to 1 November 2026 (calendar card under Events)
Restaurant Massana, a short walk towards the centre; picnic supplies from the Mercat del Lleó

quarters:Montjuïc.name: Montjuïc
quarters:Montjuïc.teaser: The wooded hill above the old town: the city's fort, a medieval cemetery and the path up to Sant Miquel
quarters:Montjuïc.story: Climb out of the Barri Vell's north-east corner and the houses stop at the slopes of Montjuïc, a hill of holm oak, terraces and broken fortifications looking straight down on the cathedral roof. The name is usually read as the hill of the Jews: the Call's medieval cemetery lay up here, and gravestones from it are now shown in the Call museum. The ruined fort on the summit was the key to every siege of the city, which is a story for its own curiosity card. From the top, paths run on into the Vall de Sant Daniel and up to the Castell de Sant Miquel.
quarters:Montjuïc.why: Go up for the view back over the old town's rooftops, the best free one in Girona.
facts: The view down over the cathedral and the Barri Vell, and the start of the hill paths
Late afternoon, with the sun behind you on the old town
The walk on to the Castell de Sant Miquel (its own card under Walks)
Nothing up here: carry cheese from Cal Formatger and bread for the top

quarters:Vall de Sant Daniel.name: Vall de Sant Daniel
quarters:Vall de Sant Daniel.teaser: Ten minutes beyond the walls the city stops: springs, plane trees and a Romanesque convent
quarters:Vall de Sant Daniel.story: Behind Montjuïc the road dips into a valley where Girona simply ends. Plane trees line a stream, kitchen gardens run along the bottom, and a string of springs, the iron-tasting Font del Ferro among them, have drawn families with picnic baskets for generations. At the top stands the Romanesque monastery of Sant Daniel, its square bell tower above the trees. In July and August, when the stone city holds the heat, this is where locals come for shade and running water. The Sant Daniel walk has its own card with the route.
quarters:Vall de Sant Daniel.why: Fill a bottle at the Font del Ferro and taste the iron for yourself.
facts: Shade, springs and kitchen gardens ten minutes from the old town
A summer morning or the hour before dusk
The Font del Ferro, and the Sant Daniel walk (its own card under Walks)
No table in the valley: bring a picnic from the Mercat del Lleó
quarters:Vall de Sant Daniel.maps_query: Vall de Sant Daniel, Girona, Spain

curiosities:The Immortal City.name: The Immortal City
curiosities:The Immortal City.teaser: Seven months under French guns in 1809, and a governor who banned the word surrender
curiosities:The Immortal City.story: Girona calls itself la immortal, and the old guides give it some twenty-five sieges in its history, taken only seven times. The one that fixed the name began in May 1809, when a French and allied army sat down below the walls. The governor, Mariano Álvarez de Castro, organised the townspeople into companies, a women's company among them, and decreed death for anyone who spoke of surrender. The city held for seven months. Famine and disease, not assault, ended it: Álvarez fell ill, handed command to Brigadier Juan Bolívar, and Girona capitulated in December. The walls have their own walk card.
curiosities:The Immortal City.why: Look at the old town from below and picture it starving behind its walls for seven months.
facts: The Museu d'Història de Girona's room on the sieges; and the Plaça de la Independència, named for the war

The capitulation is dated 10 December in Catalan sources and 12 December in English ones; the besiegers are given as anywhere from about 18,000 to 35,000, the defenders from about 3,400 regulars to some 9,000 soldiers and militia; and no single sourced count of 'twenty-five sieges' was found

curiosities:The flies of Sant Narcís.name: The flies of Sant Narcís
curiosities:The flies of Sant Narcís.teaser: The legend says flies poured out of a saint's tomb in 1285 and drove off a French army
curiosities:The flies of Sant Narcís.story: In the summer of 1285 Philip III of France laid siege to Girona on his crusade against Aragon. The legend says his soldiers broke open the tomb of Sant Narcís, the city's patron, in the church of Sant Feliu, and a swarm of flies burst out and fell on the men and their horses until the army withdrew. The history is plainer: the French did take the city that year, the Sant Feliu suburb was badly damaged, and the king fell ill at Girona and died at Perpignan in October. The fly stayed anyway, and every October it is all over the Fires de Sant Narcís (its own calendar card).
curiosities:The flies of Sant Narcís.why: Treat it as Girona does: a legend told with a straight face and a fly on every Fires poster.
facts: The chapel of Sant Narcís in the Basílica de Sant Feliu (the church has its own card); a stone fly in the old town that visitors stroke for luck, its street not confirmed this pass
Some retellings put the miracle in 1286; historians note the tomb was largely an imagined one and that the story took centuries to grow, with later fly episodes claimed for 1653 and 1808

curiosities:The cycling capital.name: The cycling capital
curiosities:The cycling capital.teaser: A small Catalan city where professional road racers outnumber tourists at the morning coffee bar
curiosities:The cycling capital.story: In the late 1990s a handful of American professionals, George Hincapie and Lance Armstrong among them, settled in Girona for its quiet back roads, and others followed. The reasons have not changed: low-traffic lanes in every direction, the Pyrenean foothills to the north, the Mediterranean about half an hour's ride east, a mild winter and an airport down the road, all cheaper than Monaco or Switzerland. Word of mouth did the rest. Today, at mid-morning, the café tables in the old town fill with team kit, and the sound is cleats on stone. La Fàbrica, a former pro's café, has its own card.
curiosities:The cycling capital.why: Sit at a café terrace mid-morning and watch the bunches roll in: the riders at the next table may be racing the Tour next summer.
facts: Café terraces in the Barri Vell at mid-morning, full of riders in team kit; La Fàbrica on Carrer de la Llebre

Nobody keeps an official count: estimates run from about 90 professionals to 'more than 100' to over 180, and a local guide told Catalan News in 2023 there may be 100 to 150 living or having lived here

sources.label: Catalan News: Cycling mecca, what makes Girona so good for bike riding

curiosities:A season of dragons on the s.name: A season of dragons on the steps
curiosities:A season of dragons on the s.teaser: In September 2015 a horse climbed the cathedral steps and Girona became King's Landing, Braavos and Oldtown
curiosities:A season of dragons on the s.story: Game of Thrones filmed in Girona in September 2015 for its sixth season, broadcast in 2016. The cathedral's Baroque staircase became the steps of the Great Sept of Baelor: the crew covered the statues and laid a surface on the stairs so Jaime Lannister could ride his horse up them. The cloister of Sant Pere de Galligants played the Citadel at Oldtown, where Samwell goes to train, and Arya's chase with the Waif ran through the old town's stairways and ended at the Arab baths. The Sept's later destruction was computer-made. Each building has its own card.
curiosities:A season of dragons on the s.why: Stand at the foot of the cathedral steps and count them before you picture the horse.
facts: The cathedral steps, the Arab baths and the cloister of Sant Pere de Galligants, all open to visit

Arya's fall into the market is placed by some on the steps of Sant Martí Sacosta, by others on the Pujada de Sant Domènec; the blind-beggar scenes are put on Carrer del Bisbe Josep Cartañà behind the cathedral

avoid:Dinner on the Plaça de la Independ.name: Dinner on the Plaça de la Independència
avoid:Dinner on the Plaça de la Independ.teaser: The arcaded square is the place for a vermouth; most of its terraces are not the place for dinner
avoid:Dinner on the Plaça de la Independ.story: The arcades of the Plaça de la Independència are one of the best places in Girona to sit, and the terraces know it. Menus in five languages, waiters at the edge of the arches and plates priced for the view, not the kitchen: set up for the day-tripper off the Barcelona train. Have the drink here, under the arches with the light going, then walk somewhere that cooks. The exception is Casa Marieta, which has been on the square since 1892 and still does duck with pears the old way.
avoid:Dinner on the Plaça de la Independ.why: Order the vermut on the square and book dinner somewhere else before you sit down.
facts: A closed rectangle of arcades lined with look-alike terraces and picture menus
A vermouth under the arcades, then dinner at Can Marquès, Fonda Cal Ros or Divinum; or, on the square itself, Casa Marieta

avoid:The paella boards by the bridges.name: The paella boards by the bridges
avoid:The paella boards by the bridges.teaser: 'Authentic paella' on a photo board by the Pont de Pedra: paella is Valencian, not from Girona
avoid:The paella boards by the bridges.story: Near the Pont de Pedra and along the riverside streets, boards on the pavement show a yellow pan, a jug of sangria and the word authentic. Paella is a Valencian dish, not a Gironí one, and a rice ready for anyone who walks by was not cooked for you. Catalan kitchens do rice their own way: dry in a flat pan, black with cuttlefish ink, or baked in a tin a la llauna, and a good one comes to the table after a proper wait. Two old houses in town still make it right.
avoid:The paella boards by the bridges.why: Ask what rice the kitchen does that day; if the answer is 'paella, any time', walk on.
facts: Pavement boards with photo menus of paella and sangria by the river bridges
The Thursday market rice at Can Marquès, beside the Mercat del Lleó; the rockfish rice a la llauna at Fonda Cal Ros

avoid:Turning up at El Celler unbooked.name: Turning up at El Celler unbooked
avoid:Turning up at El Celler unbooked.teaser: There is no walk-in at El Celler de Can Roca, and no friend of a friend at the door
avoid:Turning up at El Celler unbooked.story: Every week someone takes a taxi out to Taialà on the strength of a cancellation rumour. El Celler de Can Roca, which turns forty in 2026, takes no walk-ins: tables are booked online months ahead, the list fills fast, and the only fall-back the restaurant offers is its own waiting list. No hotel concierge or yacht agent can open a door the diary has closed. If your dates are fixed, follow the booking rule on its own card; if you are too late, the family has three other tables in and around town that you can actually get.
avoid:Turning up at El Celler unbooked.why: Book El Celler the day the window opens, and book one of the family's other tables as your back-up.
facts: A full booking system and an online waiting list, no door policy for walk-ins; closed Sunday and Monday (seen Jun 2026)

Esperit Roca at Sant Julià de Ramis, bookable about ninety days out, serving El Celler's past dishes; Normal on Plaça de l'Oli for the brothers' plain Catalan cooking; the family's original Can Roca bar in Taialà for the set lunch

avoid:Driving into the Barri Vell.name: Driving into the Barri Vell
avoid:Driving into the Barri Vell.teaser: Cameras read every plate entering the old town; three visits a quarter, then the fines arrive by post
avoid:Driving into the Barri Vell.story: The cobbled streets of the Barri Vell have long been closed to through traffic: entry needs a permit issued to residents and local businesses. At the access from Plaça Catalunya, cameras read every number plate, and a car without a permit is allowed in only three times a quarter before fines are issued automatically. The city even asked Google to stop sending satnav routes through the lanes. Since 15 September 2025 the Barri Vell also sits inside Girona's low-emission zone, enforced by camera on weekdays from 7:00 to 20:00. Above all, the streets turn into stairs without warning.
avoid:Driving into the Barri Vell.why: Leave the car on the Mercadal side and cross a footbridge; the old town is ten minutes on foot from anywhere.
facts: Camera-controlled access from Plaça Catalunya, residents and permits only; low-emission zone signs at the entrances (Oct 2026)
Park in a public car park on the west bank and walk in over the Onyar; come by train from the coast or Barcelona; check your hire car's DGT environmental label before entering the low-emission zone

follow:Fires de Sant Narcís.name: Fires de Sant Narcís
follow:Fires de Sant Narcís.teaser: Girona's own festival week: the programme for ten days of concerts, castells, fire and fairground
follow:Fires de Sant Narcís.story: The Fires de Sant Narcís are Girona's festa major, held each year at the end of October around the patron's day. In 2026 they run from 23 October to 1 November, with Sant Narcís itself on Thursday 29 October: so if you are reading this now, it is next week. The Ajuntament de Girona publishes the full programme, with three music stages, the correfoc, the human towers, havaneres on the cathedral steps and the closing fireworks. Watch it for times and changes, which shift from year to year. The festival itself has its own calendar card.
follow:Fires de Sant Narcís.why: Check the programme the morning you go: venues and times move, and the fireworks are weather-dependent.
facts: The city council's programme for Girona's festa major, 23 October to 1 November 2026 (Oct 2026)

The daily schedule: the correfoc on Plaça del Vi on Saturday 24 October, castells on Sunday 25, havaneres on the cathedral steps on Thursday 29, fireworks on 1 November (Oct 2026, from press listings; confirm on the official programme)

follow:Temps de Flors.name: Temps de Flors
follow:Temps de Flors.teaser: The festival's own channel for dates, the map and which private patios open in May
follow:Temps de Flors.story: For nine days each May, Temps de Flors fills Girona's courtyards, stairways and churches with flower installations, and private patios of the Barri Vell open to the public. The 2026 edition, the seventy-first, ran from 9 to 17 May. The organisers publish the dates, the map of installations and the list of patios ahead of each edition; the 2027 dates had not been announced when this was written. Watch the official channel from early spring if you want to plan around it, or around avoiding it. The festival itself has its own calendar card.
follow:Temps de Flors.why: Get the map as soon as it is out and walk the patios on a weekday morning.

follow:Mercat del Lleó.name: Mercat del Lleó
follow:Mercat del Lleó.teaser: The market traders' own channel: holiday closures, new stalls and special openings
follow:Mercat del Lleó.story: The Mercat del Lleó is run day to day by its traders' association, the Associació de Comerciants de la Plaça del Mercat de Girona, which manages the market's name and its social media under an agreement with the city council. That is where holiday closures, changes of hours, stall handovers and seasonal events appear first. It is worth a look before a big shop for the boat, especially around public holidays, when the market's usual Monday-to-Saturday rhythm changes. The market itself has its own card in the tables.
follow:Mercat del Lleó.why: Check it before a provisioning run on the day before a public holiday.

follow:DO Empordà.name: DO Empordà
follow:DO Empordà.teaser: The wine council's own site: every member winery, with visit times, languages and prices
follow:DO Empordà.story: The Consell Regulador of the DO Empordà, the appellation created on 19 May 1975, keeps the official register of its wineries. Each winery has a page giving when it opens for visits, how long a visit lasts, how many people it takes, the languages spoken and the price. For a crew planning a wine day inland from Girona, it is the quickest way to see who opens on which day, without phoning round. It also carries the appellation's own events through the year.
follow:DO Empordà.why: Filter by day before you drive: many cellars open for visits only at weekends.

follow:El Celler de Can Roca.name: El Celler de Can Roca
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.teaser: The restaurant's own site is the only reliable word on when the next tables open
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.story: El Celler de Can Roca releases its tables on a fixed rule, and its website states it plainly. Bookings open eleven months ahead, a new month at a time, at midnight local time on the first day of each month; a credit or debit card holds the table, and if the date is full you can join the waiting list. A no-show, or a cancellation with less than ten days' notice, is charged per person. The site also carries news from the family's other places in Girona. The restaurant has its own card in the tables.
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.why: Set an alarm for midnight Girona time on the first of the month, eleven months before your date.
